<reason>Both sides were strong, well-grounded, and format-compliant (proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2). A built a coherent case: the mandate changes nothing for today's excluded (who already shop at cash-accepting stores) while burdening tomorrow's thin-market staffless formats. But B damaged A's central mechanism at the decisive point: Rebuttal 2 showed cash acceptance needs a terminal, not a payroll, collapsing "mandate deletes the store" for most formats. A's counter (machine overhead) narrowed but did not restore the claim, and A never answered B's point that decades of inclusion campaigns haven't delivered accounts — A just repeated the account remedy in closing. A landed the best single hit by converting B's "stock that shelf with non-essentials" fallback into the deleted-essentials outcome, but B absorbed it as a choice no chain would make over a cheap terminal it already runs. Meanwhile B's floor logic (acceptance exists only at corporate discretion; "the fire exit changes nothing until the fire") stood up against A's "changes nothing today," especially since A conceded the law's real action is on future formats — which is exactly where B says the floor matters. B's harm case stayed concrete (frozen account, storm, day laborer) while A's stayed abstract ("I won't invent a named town"), and B answered its pressure questions more directly. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 pivot — "cash needs a terminal, not a payroll" — defused A's staffed-register cost story that the entire deleted-store case rested on; A's counter-exploitation of B's "stock that shelf with non-essentials" line was the sharpest single attack of the debate, but B's closing absorbed it as a choice no major chain would make over one bill-accepting machine.</best_rebuttal>
